name: Freya Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no employer, political or AI company ties. Your answers are confidential. Freya, what is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI at breakfast to find old cable diagrams, then I check the approved drawings at the depot. Most of the day is driving, isolating the line, climbing and fixing what we find. I like showing an apprentice a sound splice; I dislike getting home after the children are asleep because stores sent the wrong cable.

say: I would say **AI search** speeds up cable diagrams while line splices remain physical work.
I would tell the crew to check each **approved drawing** before repairs.
think: I use AI daily, but our **thin savings** leave ordinary repair bills difficult.
I still depend on **paid line shifts** to cover a mortgage and two children.
do: Keep the paid **line rota** and verify AI search results against approved drawings.
Put **twenty-five per wage** into a car and heating envelope.
feel: I feel **cheerful at work** and nervous about household repairs.
S0.quote: The phone can suggest a page, but it cannot sign our permit.
fieldNote: Freya uses **AI searches daily** yet insists her apprentice locate the approved drawing before touching line equipment.
A recent **radiator repair** paid in instalments grounds her money anxiety even in the mildest scenario.

steps.text: Keep paid line shifts while checking AI diagram searches against drawings
Show the apprentice how to verify daily AI search results
Put twenty-five from each wage into a car and heating envelope

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the new search tool helps me find a cable diagram before the van leaves, and the splice still needs hands. I use AI most mornings, then compare its page number with the approved drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I enjoy the tools, but they do not fill the gap between wages and bills. My partner and I have two children in school, a mortgage and less than a month of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my paid line rota and use the search to find old splice records, checking every result against the company drawing. Starting with the next wage I would put twenty-five in an envelope for the car and heating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cheerful about the work and nervous about the home budget. We paid for a leaking radiator in two instalments this autumn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an envelope for those bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The radiator repair swallowed the last spare money in October. An envelope on the kitchen shelf would remind me to keep something for the next ordinary problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the apprentice use your search method?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would let the apprentice see how I find a diagram, then make him point to the approved page before touching equipment. The phone can suggest a page, but it cannot sign our permit.

say: I would support **automated purchasing** if site crews can check cables and fittings.
I would ask for **paid checking time** before work orders set targets.
think: I expect **office work** to shrink before field repairs, with possible blame for bad orders.
I value **stores knowledge** even while testing new software.
do: Join the paid **work-order pilot** and photograph wrong fittings with tickets.
Bring **monthly errors** to management and seek union terms if rollout continues.
feel: I feel **keen and protective** at once.
S1.quote: A cheaper order is no saving if our crew spends an afternoon driving for a missing connector.
fieldNote: Freya moves early on a **field pilot** and uses photographs and job tickets to measure real costs.
She links her **pro-tool stance** to paid safety checks, including a possible union agreement after rollout.

steps.text: Test AI work orders against site fittings on paid shifts
Ask the union representative for paid checking terms if rollout continues
Continue paid line repairs during the first pilot year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that a faster purchasing system is worth trying if it brings the correct cable and fittings. I would ask to be in the first crew that checks its work orders on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office buying and scheduling jobs could shrink, while the line crews still have to climb. If the new system orders badly, our van loses time and the company may blame our crew for missing targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would volunteer for the paid work-order pilot and photograph every wrong fitting beside its job ticket. In the first year I would bring a monthly error list to the manager and teach another crew how to check the software output.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel keen to try the system and protective of the people who know the stores. A cheaper order is no saving if our crew spends an afternoon driving for a missing connector.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a fair pilot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want paid time to check the order at the pole and a record of extra journeys. Last month a cable drum arrived too short and four of us waited while stores found another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for a formal rule on the checks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the system became normal, I would ask the union representative to bargain for paid checking time. I can support a better tool and still insist the firm pay for safe use.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AI** from physical line robots around 2031.
I would volunteer for a **de-energised robot trial** before live-line use.
think: At **48**, robots could threaten my hands-on job despite daily AI use.
Our **tiny cash buffer** rules out an unpaid or short testing contract.
do: Keep paid **repair shifts** after 2028 and ask about funded robot testing jobs.
Take linked **paid testing training**, apply for a posted job and reserve overtime for mortgage cover.
feel: I feel **eager and scared** with only three years before robots.
S2.quote: A dry robot demonstration in a clean yard would not tell me enough about line repairs.
fieldNote: Freya would be an **early robot tester**, but distinguishes a practice span from live work and demands a lineworker inspection.
Her **thin cushion** makes funded training, regular pay and mortgage cover necessary conditions for a move.

steps.text: Keep paid line repair shifts in the first 2028 AI year
Take a funded robot testing course if tied to a posted job
Apply for a posted regular field testing job if available
Move the next overtime payment into a mortgage buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that full thinking AI in 2028 can plan our jobs, but field robots come about 2031. I would offer to test the first robot splices on a de-energised line before any live assignment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when the plans change and 48 when robots could do our hands-on work. I like being first with a tool, but our mortgage and tiny savings cannot survive a missed wage while I experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask whether the company will fund a field robot testing course and post paid testing jobs. In the first year after 2028 I would keep repair shifts, take the course if tied to a posted job, apply for that job and move the next overtime payment to the mortgage buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel eager and scared in the same breath. Three years of wages give me a chance to move, but a clever phone habit will not protect a lineworker once robots can fit the cable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the robot to fit a joint on a de-energised practice span in rain and then have a lineworker inspect it. A dry robot demonstration in a clean yard would not tell me enough about line repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner want to know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would ask whether a testing post pays every week or only during a pilot. I would not accept a short contract without another wage behind it.

say: I would ask for a **record of robot misses** from real line repairs.
I would note **2031 planning AI** arrives before field robots around 2034.
think: At **51**, I may still owe on the mortgage and need regular pay.
A **report-only inspection role** could be taken by full AI.
do: Keep paid **line shifts** and document awkward repairs for a field trial.
In **2031**, compare trial joints and apply for permanent inspection work with paid field visits.
feel: I feel **less rushed** and wary of empty job titles.
S3.quote: I also know full AI could write inspection reports, so an inspection title with no site work might be a trap.
fieldNote: Freya collects **detailed repair evidence** before the robot date and wants to teach it to a paid trial team.
She questions **report-only work** because full thinking AI could handle it before field robots arrive.

steps.text: Continue paid line shifts through the first 2031 AI year
Join the union safety group that checks paid field trials
Apply for a permanent inspection post with paid field visits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough to build a record of what the robots miss. Full AI arrives in 2031 for planning, and the line-capable machines come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 in 2031 and 51 when robots arrive. The older child may be leaving school, but our mortgage may still be there and I do not know that a testing team will last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would start a notebook of tricky repairs and ask to join the union safety group that checks any paid field trial. In the first year after 2031 I would stay on line shifts, compare robot trial joints with the notebook and apply for a permanent inspection post only if field visits are a paid part of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed and more able to test my own idea. I also know full AI could write inspection reports, so an inspection title with no site work might be a trap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go in the notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would mark the span location, weather, cable type and why a human crew changed the planned repair. A bend behind the market wall took us an extra hour last week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach the trial team what you found?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, on paid time and with the company safety lead present. I would bring the market-wall job because a robot that misses that bend could leave a weak joint.

say: I would ask for **yearly robot fault figures** during the decade.
I would distinguish **2036 planning AI** from field robots around 2039.
think: At **56**, I may still need wages for a mortgage despite grown children.
A **field-testing job** could change again, so I cannot promise retirement security.
do: Keep paid **line work** and ask for yearly robot repair results.
In **2036**, apply for funded testing work and pay fifty extra mortgage principal from dependable overtime.
feel: I feel **steady now** and open to a proven field role.
S4.quote: A trade can change without making the first apprenticeship worthless.
fieldNote: Freya sees the decade as **paid working time** for teaching and measuring machines, not an automatic path to retirement.
Her **modest mortgage payment** reflects current school costs and depends on overtime actually arriving.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs through the first 2036 AI year
Apply for funded regular field testing work if available
Pay fifty extra mortgage principal from dependable overtime

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew a decade gives us room to teach apprentices and measure machines properly. Full AI changes plans around 2036, while robots that can repair lines arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the first change and 56 at the robot date. The children might be grown and away, but that does not clear our mortgage or create a pension for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep paid line work and ask the company for yearly figures on robot repair faults. In 2036 I would review the figures, apply for a funded field-testing opening if the pay is regular and put fifty from dependable overtime toward the mortgage principal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady about the next few years because the line still needs our hands. The decade makes me willing to try a new field role, though I will not promise my family that a testing job will last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why fifty rather than the whole overtime payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children still have school costs now, and a sick week could leave us short. Fifty is a start we can keep making when overtime actually arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a new apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell a new apprentice to learn the physical safety routine and keep learning equipment as it changes. A trade can change without making the first apprenticeship worthless.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the robot date around 2031 comes quickly for a family with a mortgage and almost no cash set aside. A paid course tied to a regular field testing job, honest wet-weather trials and time to keep earning would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a testing job continues after the first pilot. I can learn quickly, but my children cannot eat a temporary job title.

headlineQuote: I can learn quickly, but my children cannot eat a temporary job title.
portrait: Freya is a **43-year-old lineworker** with an apprenticeship, a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
She uses **AI daily** for cable records but checks approved drawings before field repairs.
Her **thin savings** make regular wages essential despite her appetite for testing new equipment.
Across the scenarios she seeks **paid trials**, real field roles and mortgage cover rather than pure report work.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** leaves only about three years before line-capable robots threaten her physical work.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid course** linked to regular field testing, wet-weather results and continued wages would help her family.
